bio_edx.8.0.summary: Ecologists describe living things at increasing levels of organisation: an **individual** organism, a **population** of one species, a **community** of all the populations of different species, and an **ecosystem**, which is the community together with the non-living (abiotic) conditions of the place where they live. Each level contains the one below it, so a pond ecosystem contains a community, which contains many populations, which are made of individuals. Using these words precisely is essential, because mark schemes only reward the exact meaning of population, community and ecosystem.

core.h: Why we need levels of organisation
core.p: An ecosystem is complicated, so biologists break it into levels. Each level is a bigger unit that **contains the level below it**. This lets scientists ask different questions: how one organism survives, how many of one species there are, how species affect each other, or how living things interact with the physical environment.
bullets: The levels from smallest to largest: **individual, population, community, ecosystem**
Each level is made up of the level before it
Higher levels include more types of interaction
At the ecosystem level, non-living (abiotic) factors are included for the first time

callouts.p: Individual, population, community, ecosystem. Each one is contained in the next.

fig.cap: Nested levels of organisation. An individual is one organism; a population is all the organisms of one species in a habitat; a community is all the populations of different species in that habitat; an ecosystem is the community plus the abiotic conditions.

core.p: An **individual** is a single living organism, such as one oak tree, one rabbit or one bacterium. It is the smallest level of organisation in ecology.
bullets: Each individual belongs to one **species**
A species is a group of organisms that can **interbreed to produce fertile offspring**
Individuals need resources such as food, water, light, space and mates to survive and reproduce
Studying individuals tells us about adaptations, behaviour and how one organism survives

callouts.p: A group of similar organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

core.p: A **habitat** is the place where an organism lives. The idea of a habitat is needed to define the other levels, because a population and a community are always described in a particular habitat.
bullets: Examples: a pond, a rock pool, a woodland, a field, the gut of an animal
A habitat provides the resources and conditions an organism needs
Habitats can be large (an ocean) or very small (under a log)
Different habitats in the same area can hold different communities

callouts.p: The place where an organism lives.

core.p: A **population** is all the organisms of **one species** living in a habitat at the same time. All the daisies in a field form one population; all the rabbits in that field form another.
bullets: Only **one species** is included in a population
Members of a population can interbreed
Population size changes with births, deaths, immigration and emigration
Population size is affected by food, predators, disease and competition
Scientists estimate population size using sampling such as quadrats (covered in 9.5 and 9.6)

callouts.p: All the organisms of one species living in a habitat.
'All the animals in a pond' is not a population, because it contains many species.

core.p: A **community** is all the **populations of different species** living together in a habitat. It includes every living thing there: plants, animals, fungi and microorganisms.
bullets: A community contains **many species** (many populations)
It is made only of **biotic** (living) components
Populations in a community interact: they feed on each other, compete and depend on each other
Example: in a woodland, the community includes oak trees, bluebells, squirrels, owls, insects, fungi and soil bacteria
Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi are part of the community too

callouts.p: All the populations of different species living in a habitat.

core.p: An **ecosystem** is the **community** together with the **abiotic (non-living) conditions** of the environment in which it lives. It is the highest of the four main levels, and the only one that includes non-living things.
bullets: Ecosystem = community (biotic) + abiotic factors
Abiotic factors include light intensity, temperature, water, soil pH and minerals, oxygen and carbon dioxide levels, and wind
Organisms in an ecosystem interact with each other **and** with the abiotic environment
Materials such as carbon, nitrogen and water are cycled through the biotic and abiotic parts of an ecosystem
An ecosystem can be any size: a garden pond, a lake, a forest, a desert

callouts.p: A community of organisms and the abiotic (non-living) conditions in which they live, interacting together.
Population and community are living only. Ecosystem adds the abiotic environment.

core.p: The table summarises what each level contains. In an exam you may be asked to identify the level described in a sentence, so look for clue words.
bullets: 'One' organism: individual
'One species' or 'all the ... of one type': population
'Different species' or 'all the living things': community
'Living and non-living' or mentions of water, soil, temperature: ecosystem

core.p: The words **biotic** and **abiotic** are what separate a community from an ecosystem. This point only introduces them; how they affect communities is in 9.2 and 9.3.
bullets: **Biotic** = living components, such as plants, animals, fungi, bacteria, and factors like predators, food and disease
**Abiotic** = non-living components, such as light, temperature, water, pH, minerals and gases
A community contains only biotic components
An ecosystem contains biotic and abiotic components and the interactions between them

callouts.p: A-biotic means 'not living' (the prefix a- means not).

core.p: Each level affects the others. A change at one level spreads through the whole ecosystem because organisms depend on each other and on abiotic conditions.
bullets: If an individual reproduces, the **population** grows
If one population grows (for example rabbits), it affects other populations in the **community** (more food for foxes, less grass)
If an abiotic factor changes, such as a drought, many populations in the **ecosystem** are affected at once
This web of dependence is called **interdependence** (studied in 9.3)

core.p: Ecosystems do not have fixed sizes. Scientists choose the boundary that suits their question.
bullets: A rotting log, a rock pool or a garden pond can be treated as a small ecosystem
A lake, a woodland or a coral reef is a larger ecosystem
All the ecosystems on Earth together make up the **biosphere**
Large ecosystems often contain many habitats, each with its own community

core.p: Different investigations happen at different levels, which is why the terms must be used correctly when describing fieldwork.
bullets: Individual: studying adaptations of one organism to its habitat
Population: estimating how many of one species are present, for example with quadrats
Community: measuring how many different species are present (biodiversity)
Ecosystem: studying how abiotic factors such as light or soil moisture affect where species are found
Conservation decisions often need data from all levels

core.p: Questions on this point are usually short: definitions, identifying a level from a description, or explaining the difference between two levels. Precise wording earns the marks.
bullets: Population: always say **one species** and **in a habitat / area**
Community: always say **different species** or **all the populations**
Ecosystem: always mention **abiotic / non-living** factors as well as the community
When comparing two levels, state what the larger level contains that the smaller one does not
Use the example given in the question rather than a general answer

callouts.p: 'Community vs ecosystem': an ecosystem includes the abiotic (non-living) conditions; a community includes only living organisms.

analogy.p: Think of one pupil as an **individual**. All the pupils in Year 10 are like a **population**: one kind of group. Everybody in the school, including pupils, teachers, cleaners and cooks, is like a **community**: many different groups that interact. The whole school, including the people plus the buildings, heating, lighting and water supply, is like an **ecosystem**: the living community plus its non-living surroundings. The analogy breaks down because Year 10 pupils are not a separate species, and real ecosystems have no headteacher: organisms interact through feeding, competition and the cycling of materials, not through rules.

terms.d: A single living organism.
A group of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
The place where an organism lives.
All the organisms of one species living in a habitat.
All the populations of different species living in a habitat.
A community of organisms together with the abiotic conditions in which they live.
Living; biotic factors are the effects of living organisms, e.g. predators, food, disease, competition.
Non-living; abiotic factors are physical or chemical conditions, e.g. light, temperature, water, pH.
All the ecosystems on Earth together.
The way organisms in a community depend on each other for food, shelter, pollination and other needs.
An organism, such as a green plant or alga, that makes its own food by photosynthesis.
An organism that gets its energy by eating other organisms.
A microorganism such as a bacterium or fungus that breaks down dead material, returning minerals to the soil.
The variety of different species (and genetic variation within them) in an area.

mistakes.w: A population is all the animals living in an area.
mistakes.r: A population is all the organisms of **one species** in a habitat.

mistakes.w: A community is a group of the same species.
mistakes.r: A community is all the **populations of different species** in a habitat.

mistakes.w: An ecosystem is all the living things in an area.
mistakes.r: That is a community. An ecosystem is the community **plus the abiotic (non-living) conditions**.

mistakes.w: A habitat and an ecosystem are the same thing.
mistakes.r: A habitat is **the place** where an organism lives; an ecosystem is the **community and its abiotic environment interacting**.

mistakes.w: Ordering the levels as population, individual, ecosystem, community.
mistakes.r: Smallest to largest: **individual, population, community, ecosystem**.

mistakes.w: Plants are not part of the community because they do not move.
mistakes.r: A community includes **all** living organisms: plants, animals, fungi and microorganisms.

mistakes.w: Water and soil are part of the community.
mistakes.r: Water and soil are **abiotic**, so they are part of the **ecosystem**, not the community.

mistakes.w: The rabbits and the foxes in a field are one population.
mistakes.r: They are two species, so they are **two populations** within the community.

exam.q: Define the term population.
model: All the organisms of one species living in a habitat / area
exam.tip: Must include 'one species'.

exam.q: Define the term community.
model: All the populations of different species living in a habitat / area
exam.tip: Must include 'different species' or 'all populations'.

exam.q: State what is meant by an ecosystem.
model: The community / all the organisms (living in an area)
together with the abiotic / non-living conditions / environment
exam.tip: Two parts: living and non-living.

exam.q: Which of these is a population? A all the fish in a lake; B all the trout in a lake; C all the organisms in a lake; D the lake and all its organisms.
model: B
exam.tip: Look for one species.

exam.q: Place these in order from smallest to largest: community, individual, ecosystem, population.
model: Individual, population, community, ecosystem
exam.tip: Each level contains the one before.

exam.q: Explain the difference between a community and an ecosystem.
model: A community is only the living organisms / all populations of different species
an ecosystem also includes the abiotic / non-living factors such as light, temperature or water
exam.tip: Name an abiotic factor to show you know what non-living means.

exam.q: A student surveyed a rock pool and found 40 limpets, 12 crabs and some seaweed. The water temperature was 14 °C. Identify an example of a population and an example of a community from this information.
model: Population: the 40 limpets / the crabs / the seaweed (one species)
Community: limpets, crabs and seaweed together (all the organisms)
exam.tip: The temperature is abiotic, so it belongs only in the ecosystem.

exam.q: Give two abiotic factors that would be included in a description of a woodland ecosystem but not in a description of its community.
model: Any two from: light intensity, temperature, water / rainfall, soil pH, soil minerals, wind, carbon dioxide / oxygen levels
exam.tip: Abiotic factors are physical or chemical, not living.

exam.q: Explain why a change in one population can affect the whole community.
model: Organisms in a community are interdependent
e.g. a population may be food for another species / a predator
so if one population changes, the food supply or number of predators of other populations changes
these populations then change too
exam.tip: Use a food relationship example to make the chain of cause and effect clear.

exam.q: Describe the levels of organisation within a pond ecosystem, using examples. (6 marks)
model: Individual: a single organism, e.g. one frog
Population: all the organisms of one species in the pond, e.g. all the frogs
there are several populations, e.g. pondweed, water snails, fish
Community: all the populations of different species in the pond together
Ecosystem: the community plus the abiotic conditions
abiotic examples: water temperature, light, oxygen concentration, pH
each level contains the one below it / correct order individual to ecosystem
exam.tip: Give a definition and a pond example for each level, then state the order.

worked.q: Classify each of the following as individual, population, community or ecosystem: (a) one hedgehog; (b) all the bluebells in a wood; (c) all the plants, animals, fungi and bacteria in a wood; (d) a wood, including its organisms, soil, rainfall and light.
steps: (a) One organism only: individual
(b) One species (bluebells) in a habitat: population
(c) Many different species, living things only: community
(d) Living things plus abiotic factors (soil, rainfall, light): ecosystem

worked.q: A student writes: 'A field contains a community of rabbits.' Explain why this is wrong and correct it.
steps: Rabbits are one species
All the organisms of one species in a habitat form a population, not a community
A community would include all the species in the field, such as grass, rabbits, foxes and insects
Corrected sentence: 'A field contains a population of rabbits, which is part of the field community.'
worked.ans: It should be a population of rabbits, because only one species is described; a community needs many different species.

worked.q: Model answer: compare a population and an ecosystem. (3 marks)
steps: A population is all the organisms of one species in a habitat
An ecosystem contains many populations (a community), so it has many species
An ecosystem also includes abiotic / non-living factors such as temperature and water, which a population does not
worked.ans: A population is one species only and is living only; an ecosystem includes all the populations of different species plus the abiotic conditions.

bio_edx.8.1.summary: The size and distribution of populations in a community are affected by **abiotic (non-living) factors** such as temperature, light, water and pollutants, and by **biotic (living) factors** such as competition and predation. Because organisms in a community depend on each other for food, shelter, pollination and seed dispersal, they are **interdependent**: a change in one population, or in one abiotic factor, can cause knock-on changes throughout the whole community. You must be able to explain these effects with clear cause-and-effect chains and interpret data such as predator-prey graphs.

core.p: Every organism lives in conditions that help or limit its survival and reproduction. These conditions are split into two groups. The Edexcel specification names **temperature, light, water and pollutants** as abiotic factors and **competition and predation** as biotic factors.
bullets: **Abiotic factors** are non-living: physical or chemical conditions of the environment
**Biotic factors** are living: the effects of other organisms
Both types affect **population size** (how many) and **distribution** (where organisms are found)
A factor that is in short supply and restricts growth or numbers is called a **limiting factor**

callouts.p: A non-living factor in the environment that affects organisms, such as temperature, light, water or pollutants.
A living factor in the environment that affects organisms, such as competition or predation.

core.p: Temperature affects the rate of **enzyme-controlled reactions**, including photosynthesis and respiration, so it controls how fast organisms grow and which organisms can survive in a place.
bullets: Low temperatures slow enzyme activity, so plants grow more slowly and fewer organisms survive
Very high temperatures can **denature** enzymes
Organisms are adapted to a temperature range, so temperature affects **distribution**: polar bears in the Arctic, cacti in hot deserts
Rising temperatures from climate change can change where species are found, for example some species moving towards the poles or to higher altitudes
Water temperature affects how much oxygen is dissolved: warmer water holds **less oxygen**, so fewer fish may survive

core.p: Light is needed for **photosynthesis**, so light intensity affects how fast plants and algae make glucose and grow. Because plants are at the start of every food chain, light affects the whole community.
bullets: Low light intensity limits photosynthesis, so plants grow less and support fewer animals
On a woodland floor, tall trees shade the ground, so only **shade-tolerant** plants grow there
Some woodland plants, such as bluebells, grow and flower early in spring before the tree canopy blocks the light
In water, light decreases with depth, so algae and plants grow mainly near the surface
Light also affects animal behaviour, such as breeding seasons and when animals are active

core.p: All organisms need water: it is used in **photosynthesis**, keeps plant cells turgid, transports substances, and is the medium for chemical reactions in cells.
bullets: Low water availability (drought) causes plants to wilt and stop growing, reducing food for animals
Few species can survive in deserts; those that do have adaptations such as cacti storing water and having spines instead of leaves
Areas with plenty of rainfall, such as rainforests, have very high biodiversity
Flooding can also harm communities by waterlogging soil, so roots cannot get oxygen
For aquatic organisms, the water itself is the habitat, so changes in water level matter

core.p: Pollutants are harmful substances released into the environment, usually by human activity. They can kill organisms directly or change conditions so that some species cannot survive.
bullets: **Sulfur dioxide** from burning fossil fuels forms **acid rain**, which damages leaves, lowers the pH of lakes and kills fish
Excess **fertiliser** washed into rivers causes **eutrophication**: algae grow, block light, die, and decomposers use up oxygen, so fish die
Sewage in water also lowers oxygen levels as bacteria decompose it
Some species are very sensitive to pollution, so their presence or absence shows how polluted an area is (indicator species, triple topic 9.16B)
Pollution usually **reduces biodiversity** because only tolerant species survive

callouts.p: In 'explain' questions, follow every step: fertiliser, algae grow, light blocked, plants die, decomposers respire, oxygen falls, fish die.

core.p: **Competition** happens when organisms need the **same resource** and it is in **limited supply**. The better-adapted competitor gets more of the resource, so it survives and reproduces more, while the other population may decrease.
bullets: **Plants compete for**: light, water, mineral ions (from the soil) and space
**Animals compete for**: food, water, mates and territory (space)
Competition can be between individuals of the **same species** or between **different species**
Example: in the UK, **grey squirrels** (introduced from North America) outcompete native **red squirrels** for food and habitat, so red squirrel numbers have fallen
Weeds compete with crop plants, reducing crop yield
Competition affects distribution: the weaker competitor may only survive where the stronger one is absent

callouts.p: When organisms need the same resource that is in short supply, so not all can get enough.
Plants do not compete for food or carbon dioxide in GCSE answers. Say light, water, mineral ions and space.

core.p: **Predation** is when one animal (the **predator**) kills and eats another (the **prey**). Predator and prey populations affect each other, so their numbers usually rise and fall in a **cycle**.
bullets: If prey increase, predators have **more food**, survive and breed more, so predator numbers increase
More predators eat more prey, so prey numbers **decrease**
With less food, fewer predators survive, so predator numbers decrease
With fewer predators, more prey survive and breed, so prey numbers increase again
Predator peaks come **after** prey peaks (a time lag), because it takes time for predators to breed and for their young to grow
Predator populations are usually **smaller** than prey populations, because energy is lost at each trophic level
Example: snowshoe hare (prey) and lynx (predator) in Canada

callouts.p: The predator curve lags behind the prey curve because predators need time to reproduce after food becomes plentiful.

core.p: **Interdependence** means that the organisms in a community **depend on each other** to survive. If one species is removed or changes in number, it can affect many other species in the community.
bullets: Animals depend on plants and other animals for **food**
Animals depend on plants for **shelter** and **nesting materials**
Many plants depend on animals (such as bees) for **pollination**
Many plants depend on animals for **seed dispersal** (seeds carried in fur or eaten in fruit)
Plants depend on decomposers to recycle **mineral ions** into the soil, and animals add carbon dioxide used in photosynthesis
Removing one species can affect species that eat it, species it eats, and species that compete with it

callouts.p: The way organisms in a community depend on each other for resources such as food, shelter, pollination and seed dispersal, so a change in one population affects others.

core.h: Predicting changes in a food web
core.p: Exam questions often ask what happens to other populations if one species is removed or increases. Work along the arrows in both directions and consider **food** and **competition**.
bullets: If a prey species decreases, its predators have less food and may decrease, **or** they eat more of other prey species, which then decrease
If a predator is removed, its prey may increase, and then may eat more of their own food source
Species that compete for the same food may increase if a competitor is removed
Always give a reason for each change: 'because they have less food' or 'because fewer are eaten'
Using the web above: if the mice die out, foxes eat more rabbits, so rabbits decrease; owls eat more blue tits, so blue tits decrease; caterpillars may then increase

callouts.p: Effects in food webs can go more than one way. Mark schemes reward any sensible change that is explained with a reason.

core.p: In a **stable community**, the sizes of populations stay roughly constant over time because the species and the abiotic conditions are in balance. Interdependence helps keep this balance.
bullets: Predator and prey numbers fluctuate but stay within limits
Food, shelter and other resources are shared so no single species takes over
Examples of stable communities: tropical rainforests and ancient oak woodlands
Communities with **high biodiversity** are usually more stable, because if one food source is lost, consumers can switch to another
A sudden change, such as a new disease, an introduced species or pollution, can upset the balance

core.p: In real ecosystems, several factors act together, and an abiotic change usually causes biotic changes too. Grade 9 answers show these links.
bullets: A drought (abiotic) reduces plant growth, so herbivores have less food (biotic), so competition increases
Warmer water (abiotic) holds less oxygen, so oxygen-sensitive fish decline and their prey may increase
Shading by a tree (biotic) reduces light (abiotic) for plants underneath
Eutrophication links a pollutant (abiotic) with algal competition for light and decomposer activity (biotic)

callouts.p: State the factor, its direct effect on one organism, then the knock-on effect on others through food or competition.

core.p: Many questions give a graph or table of population sizes and ask you to describe or explain the pattern. Describe first, then explain using the factors above.
bullets: **Describe**: quote numbers, say when values rise, fall or peak
**Explain**: give the biological reason (more food, more predators, competition, abiotic change)
On predator-prey graphs, mention that prey peaks first and predator numbers lag behind
For distribution data (e.g. along a transect), link the change in species to a change in an abiotic factor such as light or water
Correlation between a factor and a population does not prove the factor caused the change

callouts.p: 'Describe' wants the pattern with data; 'explain' wants reasons. Doing only one loses marks.

analogy.p: A community is like a Jenga tower: every block (species) rests on and supports others. Pull out one block (remove a species) and other blocks shift or the tower may fall, which is like interdependence causing knock-on effects. The weather and the table the tower stands on are like abiotic factors: shake the table (a drought or pollution) and the whole tower is affected. The analogy breaks down because real populations can recover and grow back, species can switch to other food, and the community can rebalance over time, whereas a fallen Jenga tower stays fallen.

terms.d: A non-living factor in the environment, such as temperature, light, water or pollutants.
A living factor in the environment, such as competition, predation, food availability or disease.
All the populations of different species living in a habitat.
All the organisms of one species living in a habitat.
Where organisms are found in an area.
When organisms need the same resource that is in limited supply.
When a predator kills and eats another animal, its prey.
An animal that hunts, kills and eats other animals.
An animal that is hunted and eaten by a predator.
The way organisms in a community depend on each other, e.g. for food, shelter, pollination and seed dispersal.
A community in which population sizes stay roughly constant because species and environmental factors are in balance.
A harmful substance released into the environment, e.g. sulfur dioxide or excess fertiliser.
Excess nutrients in water cause algal growth, plant death, decomposition and oxygen loss, killing fish.
A factor in short supply that restricts the growth, size or rate of a process or population.
Transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma, often carried out by insects.
A diagram of interlinked food chains showing the feeding relationships in a community.

mistakes.w: Competition is a predator chasing its prey.
mistakes.r: Competition is when organisms need **the same limited resource**; predation is one animal **killing and eating** another.

mistakes.w: Plants compete for food and carbon dioxide.
mistakes.r: Plants compete for **light, water, mineral ions and space**.

mistakes.w: Predators and prey peak at the same time.
mistakes.r: Predator numbers peak **after** prey numbers, because of the time taken to breed (a lag).

mistakes.w: Predators increase because there are more predators.
mistakes.r: Predators increase because there is **more prey / more food**, so more survive and reproduce.

mistakes.w: Light is a biotic factor because plants need it.
mistakes.r: Light is **abiotic** (non-living); only effects of living organisms are biotic.

mistakes.w: Interdependence means animals depend on plants for food.
mistakes.r: Interdependence covers **food, shelter, pollination and seed dispersal**, in both directions, across the whole community.

mistakes.w: If the mice die, the owls will die.
mistakes.r: Owls may decrease **or switch to other prey** (e.g. blue tits), which then decrease. Give a reason for each change.

mistakes.w: Fertiliser in a river kills fish because it is poisonous.
mistakes.r: Fertiliser causes **eutrophication**: algae grow, block light, plants die, **decomposers use up oxygen**, fish die from lack of oxygen.

mistakes.w: Animals compete for light.
mistakes.r: Animals compete for **food, water, mates and territory**.

exam.q: Which of these is a biotic factor? A temperature; B light intensity; C predation; D soil pH.
model: C
exam.tip: Biotic means caused by living organisms.

exam.q: Give two abiotic factors that could affect a community of plants.
model: Any two from: temperature, light intensity, water availability, pollutants, soil pH / mineral ions
exam.tip: Name factors, not organisms.

exam.q: State two resources that plants compete for.
model: Any two from: light, water, mineral ions, space
exam.tip: Never write 'food' for plants.

exam.q: State two resources that animals compete for.
model: Any two from: food, water, mates, territory / space
exam.tip: Mates and territory are commonly missed.

exam.q: Explain how a decrease in light intensity could reduce the number of rabbits in a field.
model: Less light so less photosynthesis
grass / plants grow less
less food for rabbits so fewer rabbits survive / reproduce
exam.tip: Link the abiotic factor to the producer first, then to the consumer.

exam.q: Explain why the predator population peaks after the prey population on a predator-prey graph.
model: Predators need time to reproduce / for young to grow after food increases
so predator numbers rise only after prey numbers have risen
exam.tip: Use the word 'lag' or explain the delay.

exam.q: Describe and explain the changes in a predator-prey cycle.
model: Prey numbers increase so more food for predators
predator numbers increase (after a delay)
more prey eaten so prey numbers decrease
less food so predator numbers decrease, then prey increase again
exam.tip: Four linked steps, each with a reason.

exam.q: Grey squirrels were introduced to the UK. Explain why the number of red squirrels decreased.
model: Grey and red squirrels compete for the same food / habitat / resources
grey squirrels are better competitors / get more of the resources
so fewer red squirrels survive and reproduce
exam.tip: Name the type of biotic factor: competition.

exam.q: Explain what is meant by interdependence, using an example.
model: Organisms in a community depend on each other (for food, shelter, pollination, seed dispersal)
valid example, e.g. bees pollinate flowers and get nectar / birds nest in trees
exam.tip: Give a specific example, not just a definition.

exam.q: Fertiliser from a farm runs into a river. Explain how this could cause fish in the river to die.
model: Nutrients (nitrates) cause rapid growth of algae
algae block light so water plants cannot photosynthesise and die
decomposers / bacteria break down dead plants and algae and respire
oxygen in the water decreases so fish die
exam.tip: Every step in the chain is a mark.

exam.q: In a woodland, a disease kills most of the mice. Using a food web containing grass, oak trees, rabbits, mice, caterpillars, blue tits, foxes and owls, explain the effects on other organisms in the community. (6 marks)
model: Foxes and owls have less food so their numbers may decrease
foxes may eat more rabbits so rabbit numbers decrease
owls may eat more blue tits so blue tit numbers decrease
fewer blue tits so caterpillar numbers increase
caterpillars eat more oak leaves so oak trees may be damaged
less grass / acorns eaten by mice so grass may increase / rabbits have less competition
this shows interdependence: a change in one population affects many others
exam.tip: Work outwards from the mice along every arrow and give a reason for each change.

worked.q: Model answer: a stream receives sulfur dioxide pollution in acid rain. Explain how this could change the community.
steps: Sulfur dioxide dissolves in rainwater to form acid rain, which lowers the pH of the stream
Many organisms, e.g. fish and some invertebrates, cannot survive at low pH, so their populations decrease
Animals that feed on them have less food, so their populations may also decrease
Only pollution-tolerant species survive, so biodiversity in the community falls
This is an abiotic factor causing biotic knock-on effects through interdependence
worked.ans: The acidic water kills sensitive species, so their predators lose food, tolerant species dominate, and biodiversity decreases.

worked.q: A table shows a lynx population of 20 when the hare population is 80 000, rising to 60 lynx two years after the hares peak at 150 000. Describe and explain this pattern.
steps: Describe: the hare population increases from 80 000 to 150 000, and the lynx population increases from 20 to 60
The lynx peak comes about two years after the hare peak
Explain: more hares means more food for lynx, so more lynx survive and breed
The delay happens because lynx take time to breed and for young to mature
Lynx numbers are always much smaller because energy is lost between trophic levels, so fewer predators can be supported
worked.ans: Lynx numbers rise after hare numbers rise because of more food, with a two-year lag caused by the time needed to reproduce.

worked.q: Model answer: bluebells grow on the floor of an oak woodland. Explain why most bluebells flower in early spring.
steps: Bluebells need light for photosynthesis
In summer the oak trees have full leaves, which shade the woodland floor (competition for light)
In early spring the oak leaves have not fully opened, so more light reaches the ground
Bluebells can photosynthesise, grow and flower before the canopy closes
worked.ans: They flower early to get enough light before the oak canopy shades them, avoiding competition with the trees for light.

bio_edx.8.2.summary: Some organisms cannot survive on their own: their survival depends on a close relationship with another species. In **parasitism** one organism (the parasite) lives on or in a host and benefits while the host is harmed, as with fleas, head lice, tapeworms and mistletoe. In **mutualism** both species benefit, as with oxpeckers, cleaner fish and nitrogen-fixing bacteria in legume root nodules. For the exam you must name the examples, say who benefits and how, and explain why each relationship affects survival.

core.h: Survival can depend on other species
core.p: All organisms in a community are **interdependent**, but some relationships are much closer than simply eating or being eaten. In parasitism and mutualism two different species live in very close contact for long periods, and at least one of them needs the other to survive.
bullets: Both are relationships **between two different species**
In **parasitism** only one species benefits and the other is harmed
In **mutualism** both species benefit
A quick code: parasitism is (+ / -), mutualism is (+ / +)
These relationships mean a change in one population changes the other population too
If the host or partner disappears, the dependent species may not survive

callouts.p: Parasitism: fleas, head lice, tapeworms, mistletoe. Mutualism: oxpeckers, cleaner fish, nitrogen-fixing bacteria in legumes. Learn all seven by name.

core.p: A **parasite** lives on or inside another living organism, called the **host**, and takes food or other resources from it. The parasite gains, but the host loses nutrients, is damaged, or may catch diseases. A successful parasite usually does not kill its host quickly, because it relies on the host staying alive to keep feeding it.
bullets: **Ectoparasites** live on the outside of the host (fleas, head lice)
**Endoparasites** live inside the host (tapeworms)
Plants can be parasites too (mistletoe takes water and minerals from trees)
Parasites have adaptations to attach to the host and get food from it
The host may become weaker, so it is more likely to be eaten, catch disease or compete less well
Parasites often have huge numbers of offspring because the chance of reaching a new host is small

callouts.p: A relationship between two species where one organism (the parasite) lives on or in another (the host), gaining nutrients or shelter, and the host is harmed.

core.p: Fleas are small wingless insects that live in the fur or feathers of mammals and birds such as dogs, cats and rats. They are **ectoparasites** that feed on the host's **blood**.
bullets: Piercing mouthparts break the host's skin to suck blood
**Benefit to flea:** a food supply (blood) and a warm place to live and breed
**Harm to host:** loss of blood, itching, irritated skin and sores from scratching
Fleas can carry **pathogens** from one host to another (rat fleas spread the bacteria that cause plague)
Body is flattened side to side so it moves easily between hairs
Powerful back legs let fleas jump onto new hosts

callouts.p: For 'how does the flea benefit', the mark is for feeding on the host's blood, not just 'getting food'.

core.p: Head lice are tiny insects that live only on the human scalp. They are **ectoparasites** that feed by sucking small amounts of **blood** from the scalp, several times a day.
bullets: Claws grip tightly to hair shafts so they are not easily removed
Females glue their eggs (**nits**) to hairs close to the scalp, where it is warm
They spread by **head-to-head contact** with an infested person
**Benefit to louse:** food (blood), warmth and shelter
**Harm to host:** itching and irritation of the scalp; scratching can lead to infection
They cannot survive long away from a human host, which shows how dependent they are

core.p: Tapeworms are flat, ribbon-like worms that live in the **small intestine** of animals such as humans, pigs and cattle. They are **endoparasites**. They have no gut of their own; instead they **absorb digested food** from the host's intestine straight through their body surface.
bullets: The head (**scolex**) has **hooks and suckers** that attach firmly to the gut wall so it is not swept away
A long flat body made of segments (**proglottids**) gives a **large surface area** for absorbing food
The outer surface resists the host's **digestive enzymes**, so the worm is not digested
Mature segments full of eggs break off and leave in the host's faeces
Humans can be infected by eating **undercooked meat** that contains tapeworm larvae
**Benefit to tapeworm:** a constant supply of digested food in a warm, protected place
**Harm to host:** the host loses nutrients, so it may lose weight, become malnourished and have abdominal pain

callouts.p: A tapeworm does not eat the host's gut. It absorbs the host's already digested food, so the host is deprived of nutrients.

core.p: Mistletoe is a **parasitic plant** that grows on the branches of trees such as apple and poplar. It has green leaves and can photosynthesise, but it does not have its own roots in the soil. Instead it grows special structures called **haustoria** into the host's branch and taps into the **xylem**.
bullets: Haustoria push into the branch and connect with the host's xylem
**Benefit to mistletoe:** it takes **water and mineral ions** from the host tree
Growing high on branches also puts its leaves in the light
Because it can photosynthesise it is sometimes called a **partial parasite**
**Harm to host:** the tree loses water and minerals, so heavily infected branches grow less well and may die
Birds eat the sticky berries and spread the seeds to new trees

callouts.p: If a question asks for a plant that is a parasite, mistletoe is the spec answer. Say it takes water and mineral ions from the host.

core.p: In **mutualism** two species live closely together and **both benefit**. Each partner provides something the other needs, such as food, protection, cleaning or nutrients. Because both gain, natural selection favours individuals that cooperate, and the relationship can become essential to one or both species.
bullets: Both species gain something, so it is (+ / +)
Benefits often include **food**, **removal of parasites**, **shelter** or **nutrients**
The partners may be very different (a bird and a buffalo, bacteria and a plant)
Learn three spec examples: oxpeckers, cleaner fish and nitrogen-fixing bacteria
In an answer, always state the benefit to **each** species separately

callouts.p: A relationship between two different species in which both organisms benefit.

core.p: Oxpeckers are birds found in Africa that perch on large grazing mammals such as buffalo, rhinos and zebras. They feed on **ticks** and other parasites living on the mammal's skin.
bullets: **Benefit to oxpecker:** a reliable source of **food** (ticks, other parasites)
**Benefit to mammal:** **parasites are removed**, so less blood loss and less risk of infection
Oxpeckers also make loud alarm calls when predators approach, warning the host
Note the double link: ticks are parasites of the buffalo, and the oxpecker relationship removes them
Some scientists have observed oxpeckers pecking at wounds, so the benefit to the host may not always be complete, but the exam answer is mutualism

core.p: Cleaner fish, such as cleaner wrasse, live on coral reefs at places called **cleaning stations**. Larger fish visit them and allow the small cleaner fish to swim over their bodies, and even inside their mouths and gills, without eating them.
bullets: **Benefit to cleaner fish:** **food**, by eating parasites, dead skin and bits of food
**Benefit to larger fish:** **parasites and dead skin are removed**, reducing infection and damage
The larger fish does not eat the cleaner, which shows the relationship is stable
Both species benefit, so this is mutualism, not predation

callouts.p: The cleaner fish is not a predator of the parasites in a mark-scheme sense; the key point is that the cleaner gets food and the host is cleaned. Both benefit.

core.p: Legumes are plants such as **peas, beans and clover**. Their roots have swellings called **root nodules** that contain **nitrogen-fixing bacteria**. Plants cannot use nitrogen gas from the air, but they need nitrogen to make **amino acids and proteins**. The bacteria solve this problem.
bullets: The bacteria **fix nitrogen**: they convert **nitrogen gas (N2)** from the air in the soil into **nitrogen compounds** (ammonium ions) the plant can use
**Benefit to plant:** a supply of nitrogen compounds to make **amino acids, proteins** and DNA, so it grows well
**Benefit to bacteria:** **sugars (carbohydrates)** made by the plant in photosynthesis, used for respiration, plus a protected place to live
This means legumes can grow well in **nitrogen-poor soil** where other plants struggle
When legumes die and decay, the nitrogen compounds are added to the soil, which is why farmers use them in crop rotation

callouts.p: Bacteria give the plant nitrogen compounds; the plant gives the bacteria sugars. Learn it as a two-way exchange.

core.p: Exam questions often give a new example and ask you to decide which relationship it is. Ask: does the second species benefit or is it harmed? If harmed, it is parasitism; if it benefits, it is mutualism.
bullets: Parasite + host = one gains, one loses
Mutualistic partners = both gain
In both, the species live in close contact for a long time
Parasites depend on the host; in mutualism each partner may depend on the other
Predation is different: the predator kills and eats its prey quickly

head: Example
Type
Who benefits and how
Effect on other species
rows: Host loses blood, itches, may get disease
Host has parasites, dead skin removed

core.p: Because parasites and mutualists are so closely linked to another species, their population sizes are linked too. This is a grade 9 way to connect this point to interdependence.
bullets: If the host population falls, the parasite population falls because there are fewer hosts to feed on
A large parasite population can reduce the host population by weakening or killing hosts
If ticks decline, oxpecker numbers may fall because they lose their food source
If legumes are removed, the nitrogen-fixing bacteria lose their sugar supply and protected home
Removing a mutualistic partner can reduce the growth or survival of the other species
Explain with a chain: change in one species, so change in resource, so change in survival of the other

callouts.p: For each example: name it, say whether it is parasitism or mutualism, give the benefit to one species, then the harm or benefit to the other.

analogy.t: The freeloading lodger and the business partners
analogy.p: A parasite is like a lodger who moves into your house, eats your food and pays nothing: they do well and you are worse off, but they need you to keep living there. Mutualism is like two shops doing a trade deal: the baker gives the farmer bread and the farmer gives the baker flour, so both are better off. The analogy breaks down because organisms do not choose or agree to these relationships; they evolved over many generations by natural selection, and a parasite's harm can include spreading disease, which a lodger does not.

terms.d: The way organisms in a community depend on each other for food, shelter, pollination, seed dispersal and other needs.
A relationship where one organism lives on or in a host and benefits, while the host is harmed.
An organism that lives on or in another living organism and takes nutrients or resources from it.
The organism that a parasite lives on or in, and which is harmed by it.
A parasite that lives on the outside of its host, such as a flea or head louse.
A parasite that lives inside its host, such as a tapeworm in the intestine.
A relationship between two different species in which both organisms benefit.
The head of a tapeworm, with hooks and suckers that attach it to the host's gut wall.
One of the segments making up a tapeworm's body; mature ones contain eggs.
Structures that mistletoe grows into a host branch to take water and mineral ions from its xylem.
A plant in the pea and bean family, such as clover, that has root nodules containing nitrogen-fixing bacteria.
A swelling on the root of a legume that contains nitrogen-fixing bacteria.
The conversion of nitrogen gas from the air into nitrogen compounds, such as ammonium ions, that plants can use.
A place on a reef where cleaner fish remove parasites and dead skin from larger fish.
An organism, such as a flea, that carries a pathogen from one host to another.

mistakes.w: Mutualism is when one organism helps another.
mistakes.r: Mutualism is a relationship between two different species where both organisms benefit.

mistakes.w: Parasites kill their host.
mistakes.r: Parasites harm the host, for example by taking nutrients; they usually depend on the host staying alive.

mistakes.w: The tapeworm eats the intestine.
mistakes.r: The tapeworm absorbs the host's digested food through its body surface, so the host loses nutrients.

mistakes.w: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria give the plant nitrogen gas.
mistakes.r: The bacteria convert nitrogen gas into nitrogen compounds (ammonium ions) that the plant uses to make amino acids and proteins.

mistakes.w: The plant gives the bacteria nitrogen.
mistakes.r: The plant gives the bacteria sugars (carbohydrates) made in photosynthesis.

mistakes.w: Mistletoe is not a parasite because it makes its own food.
mistakes.r: Mistletoe is a parasite because it takes water and mineral ions from the host tree's xylem, harming the tree.

mistakes.w: Oxpeckers and buffalo are an example of parasitism.
mistakes.r: It is mutualism: the oxpecker gets food (ticks) and the buffalo has parasites removed.

mistakes.w: Fleas live inside the host.
mistakes.r: Fleas and head lice are ectoparasites that live on the outside of the host and feed on blood.

mistakes.w: Only giving the benefit to one species in a mutualism question.
mistakes.r: State the benefit to each species separately to get both marks.

exam.q: State what is meant by mutualism.
model: A relationship between two (different) species in which both benefit
exam.tip: Both and two species are the key words.

exam.q: Which of these is an example of a parasite: oxpecker, cleaner fish, head louse, clover?
model: Head louse
exam.tip: Learn the four spec parasites: fleas, head lice, tapeworms, mistletoe.

exam.q: Describe how a tapeworm benefits from living in the human intestine.
model: Absorbs digested food / nutrients from the intestine
Warm / protected environment / constant food supply
exam.tip: Say absorbs digested food, not eats.

exam.q: Explain how a tapeworm harms its host.
model: Takes / absorbs nutrients from the host's food
So the host is deprived of nutrients / loses weight / malnourished
exam.tip: Give the cause and the consequence.

exam.q: Explain why the relationship between oxpeckers and buffalo is described as mutualism.
model: Oxpecker gets food by eating ticks / parasites
Buffalo has parasites removed (so both benefit)
exam.tip: One mark for each species.

exam.q: Explain how fleas are adapted to be parasites.
model: Piercing mouthparts to suck blood
Strong legs to jump onto host / flattened body to move through fur
exam.tip: Link each feature to its job.

exam.q: Mistletoe has green leaves. Explain why it is still described as a parasite.
model: It takes water and mineral ions from the host tree / from xylem
Host tree is harmed / grows less well
exam.tip: Mention the host is harmed: that is what makes it parasitism.

exam.q: Explain how legumes and nitrogen-fixing bacteria both benefit from their relationship.
model: Bacteria live in root nodules
Bacteria convert nitrogen (gas) into nitrogen compounds / ammonium
Plant uses these to make amino acids / proteins
Plant supplies bacteria with sugars / carbohydrates (from photosynthesis)
exam.tip: Two marks per partner: what is given and what it is used for.

exam.q: Clover grows well in soil low in nitrates, but grass does not. Explain why.
model: Clover is a legume with nitrogen-fixing bacteria in root nodules
Bacteria provide nitrogen compounds so clover can make proteins without nitrates from soil
exam.tip: Link the bacteria to the missing nitrates.

exam.q: Discuss how the survival of some organisms depends on other species. Use examples of parasitism and mutualism in your answer.
model: Parasitism: one species benefits, host is harmed
Tapeworm absorbs digested food in intestine, host loses nutrients
Flea / head louse feeds on host blood, causing itching / disease
Mistletoe takes water and minerals from host tree
Mutualism: both species benefit
Oxpecker / cleaner fish gets food, host has parasites removed
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria give legume nitrogen compounds, plant gives sugars
Parasite cannot survive without host / loss of partner reduces survival
exam.tip: Cover at least two examples of each type and say what each species gains or loses.

worked.q: A student reads: 'A remora fish attaches to a shark and eats scraps of food the shark drops; the shark is not affected.' Is this parasitism or mutualism?
steps: Step 1: identify the two species: remora and shark
Step 2: effect on remora: it benefits (gets food)
Step 3: effect on shark: no benefit and no harm
Step 4: parasitism needs the host to be harmed; mutualism needs both to benefit
Step 5: neither condition is met, so it is neither
worked.ans: It is neither parasitism nor mutualism, because the shark is neither harmed nor helped. Always check the effect on both species before choosing.

worked.q: A farmer notices pea plants grow well in a field where wheat grew poorly. Use your knowledge of mutualism to explain the difference.
steps: Peas are legumes with root nodules containing nitrogen-fixing bacteria
The bacteria convert nitrogen gas from soil air into nitrogen compounds (ammonium)
The peas use these to make amino acids and proteins for growth
In return the peas supply the bacteria with sugars from photosynthesis
Wheat has no nodules, so it relies on nitrates in the soil, which are low
worked.ans: The peas get nitrogen compounds from their mutualistic bacteria, so they can make proteins and grow even in nitrate-poor soil, whereas the wheat cannot.

bio_edx.8.3.summary: This core practical uses **quadrats** and **belt transects** to find out how the distribution and abundance of organisms is linked to abiotic factors such as light intensity, soil moisture, pH and temperature. **Random sampling** with quadrats is used to compare two different areas without bias, while a **belt transect** is used to see how organisms change gradually across a habitat, for example from the shade of a tree into an open field. You must be able to describe the method, explain why each step is done, identify variables, analyse results as a correlation and suggest improvements.

core.p: Ecologists want to know **why organisms live where they do**. It is impossible to count every plant in a field, so we take **samples** and use them to represent the whole area. This practical links the **distribution** (where organisms are found) and **abundance** (how many there are) of a species to the **abiotic factors** in its environment.
bullets: **Distribution**: where a species is found in a habitat
**Abundance**: how many individuals there are, or how much of the ground they cover
Two main techniques: **quadrats** with **random sampling**, and **belt transects**
Random sampling compares **two separate areas** (e.g. a shaded lawn and a sunny lawn)
A belt transect shows **change across a gradient** (e.g. from tree shade to open ground, or down a seashore)
At each sample point you also **measure an abiotic factor** so you can look for a relationship

callouts.p: Investigate the relationship between organisms and their environment using field-work techniques, including quadrats and belt transects.

core.p: Most of the equipment is simple, but you must be able to say what each item is used for.
bullets: **Quadrat**: a square frame, often 0.5 m x 0.5 m (area 0.25 m2), sometimes divided into a grid
**Two tape measures**: laid at right angles to make a grid for random sampling, or one tape laid as the transect line
**Random number generator** (calculator or table): to choose coordinates
**Identification key** or field guide: to identify the species correctly
**Light meter**: measures light intensity
**Soil moisture meter**: measures how wet the soil is
**pH probe or soil pH kit**: measures soil pH
**Thermometer or temperature probe**: measures air or soil temperature
Clipboard and results table to record data

core.p: A **quadrat** marks out a fixed, known area of ground so that the same area is sampled every time. Inside it you either **count** the number of individuals of a species, or estimate the **percentage cover** if individuals are hard to count (like grass or moss).
bullets: Place the quadrat flat on the ground at the chosen point
**Count** the number of individuals of the species inside the quadrat, or
Estimate **percentage cover**: count the grid squares that are more than half covered by the species
In a 25-square quadrat each square is 4%; in a 100-square quadrat each square is 1%
Use a rule for plants on the edge, such as count them only if more than half is inside, or count those touching two sides only
Record **presence or absence** if you only want to know how often a species is found (frequency)

callouts.p: Saying you will use the same rule for plants on the edge of every quadrat is a common method mark, because it keeps the counting consistent.

core.h: Random sampling to compare two areas
core.p: To compare two areas, such as a sunny part and a shaded part of a school field, quadrats must be placed **randomly** in each area. This avoids **bias**, where you might choose spots that look interesting or have lots of plants.
bullets: Lay two **tape measures at right angles** along two edges of the area to make a grid
Use a **random number generator** to pick two numbers: these are the **coordinates** for the quadrat
Place the bottom left corner of the quadrat at those coordinates
Count the organisms or estimate percentage cover
Repeat for a **large number of quadrats** (e.g. 10 or more) in each area
Calculate the **mean** number per quadrat for each area and compare them
Measure the abiotic factor (e.g. light intensity) at each quadrat too

callouts.p: Placing quadrats at positions chosen by chance, for example using random coordinates, so that every part of the area has an equal chance of being sampled and the results are not biased.

core.h: Why sampling must be random and repeated
core.p: The whole point of sampling is that the samples should **represent the whole area**. Two things make that more likely: choosing positions at random, and taking enough samples.
bullets: **Random** positions remove **bias** from the person choosing where to sample
**Many** quadrats reduce the effect of any one unusual quadrat (an anomaly) on the mean
More samples make the mean **more representative** and the conclusion more valid
Using the **same size quadrat** in both areas makes the comparison fair
Sampling both areas at the **same time of day** and in similar weather keeps conditions comparable
Calculating a **mean** allows areas sampled with the same number of quadrats to be compared directly

callouts.p: Throwing a quadrat over your shoulder is not truly random and can be unsafe. The mark scheme wants random coordinates from a random number generator.

core.p: A **transect** is a line across a habitat where conditions change gradually, such as from under a tree into open grass, or from the sea up a rocky shore. A **belt transect** places quadrats along this line so you can see how the abundance of a species changes as an abiotic factor changes.
bullets: Lay a tape measure in a straight line across the habitat, through the **gradient** you are studying
Place a quadrat at **regular intervals** along the tape (e.g. every 2 m); placing them next to each other is a **continuous** belt transect
In each quadrat, count the organisms or estimate percentage cover
At each quadrat, **measure the abiotic factor** (e.g. light intensity, soil moisture)
**Repeat** the transect in several different places parallel to the first and calculate means
Plot number of organisms (or percentage cover) and the abiotic factor against **distance**

callouts.p: A belt transect uses systematic sampling at regular intervals, not random sampling, because you want to follow a change across the habitat.

core.p: To find a relationship you must measure the abiotic factor **at every quadrat**, not just once for the whole area. Each factor needs the right instrument and a consistent technique.
bullets: Take readings at the **same height** and position in each quadrat (e.g. light meter at ground level, facing up)
Take readings at about the **same time** so conditions such as cloud cover do not change between quadrats
Take **repeat readings** at each quadrat and calculate a mean
Electronic probes give more **precise** readings than colour-based kits

head: Abiotic factor
Equipment
Good technique
rows: Hold at ground level, same direction, avoid your shadow
Push probe to the same depth each time
pH probe or soil pH kit
Same depth of soil; compare kit colour with chart
Same depth or height; leave to settle before reading

core.p: Field work is harder to control than lab work because you cannot control the weather or the soil. You must still identify the variables and explain how you keep conditions as similar as possible.
bullets: **Independent variable**: the abiotic factor or position (e.g. distance from tree, light intensity)
**Dependent variable**: number of a species per quadrat, or percentage cover
**Control variables**: same quadrat size, same species identified with a key, same counting rule, same time of day, same method for each abiotic reading
**Uncontrolled variables**: weather, trampling, grazing, other abiotic factors that also change along the transect
Because other factors cannot be controlled, conclusions must be made carefully

callouts.p: 'Keep it fair' gets no marks. Write 'use the same size quadrat at each point' or 'take readings at the same time of day'.

core.p: After collecting the data, calculate **means** for each area or each distance and draw a graph. For a transect, plot distance on the x-axis with species abundance and the abiotic factor on the y-axes, so you can see whether they rise and fall together.
bullets: Random sampling: compare the **mean** number per quadrat in each area
Transect: plot a **line graph or bar chart** of abundance against distance
Describe the **trend** using data: e.g. number of daisies rises from 2 at 0 m to 20 at 10 m
A **positive correlation** means both increase together; a **negative correlation** means one increases as the other decreases
State whether the trend supports your hypothesis
**Correlation is not causation**: other factors such as soil moisture may also change

callouts.p: If daisies increase as light increases, you can say they are correlated. To claim light causes the change you would need to rule out other factors that vary along the transect.

core.p: Field data is never perfect. Being able to spot sources of error and suggest specific improvements is a common source of marks.
bullets: **Misidentifying species**: use an identification key or photo guide
**Inconsistent counting** at quadrat edges: agree one counting rule
**Percentage cover is subjective**: use a quadrat with more grid squares, or have the same person estimate each time
**Too few quadrats**: increase the number of quadrats or repeat transects to make the mean more representative
**Abiotic factors change** during the day (e.g. clouds): take readings at the same time, or take several and use a mean
**Other factors vary** along a transect: measure several abiotic factors to see which correlates best
Identify and exclude or re-check **anomalous** results

core.h: Safety and ethics in field work
core.p: Field work has different hazards from the lab, and you also have a responsibility not to damage the habitat you are studying.
bullets: Wash hands after handling soil or plants
Watch for hazards such as uneven ground, water, tides on a shore, or stinging plants
Wear suitable clothing and footwear
Do not remove or trample plants and animals more than necessary
Return any organisms or stones you move to where you found them
Work in groups and tell someone where you are

callouts.p: In a 6 mark method question, a safety point is rarely needed. Spend your marks on placing quadrats, counting, measuring the abiotic factor and repeating.

analogy.t: Taste-testing a giant pot of soup
analogy.p: You cannot drink a whole pot of soup to see if it is salty, so you taste a few spoonfuls from different places. Quadrats are the spoonfuls: small samples that represent the whole field. Random sampling is like stirring before tasting so you do not just taste the top, and taking more spoonfuls gives a better idea of the whole pot. A belt transect is like tasting spoonfuls in a line from the hot middle to the cooler edge to see how the soup changes. The analogy breaks down because soup can be stirred until it is the same everywhere, whereas a habitat really is different from place to place, which is exactly what you are trying to measure.

A line across a habitat along which quadrats are placed at regular intervals to study how organisms change across a gradient.

Choosing sample positions by chance, e.g. with random coordinates, so the results are not biased.
Taking samples at regular intervals, such as every 2 m along a transect.
Where a species is found within a habitat.
How many individuals of a species are present, or how much area they cover.
The percentage of the area inside a quadrat that is covered by a particular species.
A non-living factor in the environment, such as light intensity, temperature, soil moisture or pH.
An instrument that measures light intensity.
A systematic error caused by choosing samples in a non-random way, so results do not represent the whole area.
The total of the values divided by the number of values, used to summarise data from many quadrats.
A relationship between two variables where a change in one is linked to a change in the other.
A sample that accurately reflects the whole area being studied.
A series of questions or descriptions used to identify organisms correctly.

mistakes.w: Throw the quadrat randomly over your shoulder.
mistakes.r: Use a random number generator to produce coordinates on a grid made by two tape measures at right angles.

mistakes.w: Repeat it to make it more accurate.
mistakes.r: Use more quadrats or repeat transects so the mean is more representative / repeatable.

mistakes.w: Place quadrats randomly along a transect.
mistakes.r: In a belt transect, quadrats are placed at regular intervals along the tape measure.

mistakes.w: Measure light intensity once for the whole area.
mistakes.r: Measure the abiotic factor in or at every quadrat so it can be matched to the count.

mistakes.w: Keep it a fair test.
mistakes.r: Name the control: same quadrat size, same time of day, same counting rule, same height for the light meter.

mistakes.w: More light causes more daisies.
mistakes.r: There is a positive correlation between light intensity and daisy numbers; other factors may also be involved.

mistakes.w: Use a thermometer to measure light.
mistakes.r: Use a light meter for light intensity, a soil moisture meter for moisture and a pH probe for pH.

mistakes.w: Count all the plants in the field.
mistakes.r: Take samples with quadrats because it is impractical to count every organism.

exam.q: Name the piece of equipment used to measure light intensity in a habitat.
model: Light meter
exam.tip: Learn one instrument for each abiotic factor.

exam.q: State why quadrats should be placed randomly when comparing two areas.
model: To avoid bias / so the sample is representative
exam.tip: The word bias usually earns the mark.

exam.q: Describe how random coordinates are used to place a quadrat.
model: Lay two tape measures at right angles to form a grid
Use a random number generator to give coordinates for the quadrat position
exam.tip: Both the grid and the random numbers are needed.

exam.q: Explain why a student should use at least ten quadrats in each area.
model: Reduces the effect of anomalous / unusual quadrats
So the mean is more representative of the area
exam.tip: Link number of samples to a representative mean.

exam.q: A student estimated percentage cover in a 100-square quadrat. Give one reason why this estimate may not be accurate, and one improvement.
model: Estimate is subjective / hard to judge part-covered squares
Use same rule for part-covered squares / same person for all estimates
exam.tip: Pair the problem with a matching fix.

exam.q: Give two variables that should be controlled when measuring light intensity along a transect.
model: Height / position of light meter
Time of day / same weather conditions
exam.tip: Be specific to light.

exam.q: Describe how a belt transect could be used to investigate the distribution of a plant from under a tree into an open field.
model: Lay a tape measure from the tree trunk into the open field
Place quadrats at regular intervals along the tape, e.g. every 2 m
Count the number of plants / estimate percentage cover in each quadrat
Measure light intensity at each quadrat with a light meter
Repeat the transect in other positions and calculate means
exam.tip: Include placing, counting, measuring and repeating.

exam.q: A student found a positive correlation between daisy numbers and light intensity along a transect. Explain why she cannot conclude that light intensity causes the change in daisy numbers.
model: Other abiotic factors (e.g. soil moisture / temperature) also change along the transect
These were not controlled / measured, so could be the cause
exam.tip: Name a specific other factor.

exam.q: Explain why a belt transect uses regular intervals rather than random sampling.
model: To show how distribution changes across a gradient / with distance
Random positions might miss parts of the gradient
exam.tip: Transect = change along a line.

exam.q: Plan an investigation to find out whether the number of dandelions differs between a sunny area and a shaded area of a school field.
model: Mark out each area with two tape measures at right angles
Use random number generator to choose coordinates
Place a quadrat (e.g. 0.5 m x 0.5 m) at each coordinate
Count the number of dandelions in each quadrat
Use at least 10 quadrats in each area
Measure light intensity at each quadrat with a light meter
Use same size quadrat / same counting rule / same time of day
Calculate the mean number per quadrat in each area and compare
exam.tip: A logical sequence with a control and a mean gets top marks.

worked.q: A student used a 25-square quadrat. Moss filled 6 squares completely, and 4 more squares were more than half covered. Calculate the percentage cover of moss.
steps: Each square = 100% / 25 = 4%
Count squares more than half covered: 6 + 4 = 10 squares
Percentage cover = 10 x 4% = 40%

worked.q: Along a transect from a hedge, the mean number of buttercups per quadrat was 1, 3, 6, 9 and 12 at 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8 m. Light intensity rose from 200 to 1000 lux. Describe and explain the pattern, and suggest one improvement.
steps: Describe: buttercup numbers increase as distance from the hedge increases, from 1 to 12
Link: light intensity also increases with distance, so there is a positive correlation
Explain: more light means more photosynthesis, so buttercups can grow and reproduce more in brighter places
Caution: other factors such as soil moisture may also change, so light may not be the only cause
Improvement: repeat the transect in several places and measure soil moisture at each quadrat too
worked.ans: There is a positive correlation between buttercup numbers and light intensity, probably because light is needed for photosynthesis; repeat the transect and measure other abiotic factors to strengthen the conclusion.

bio_edx.8.4.summary: Counting every organism in a habitat is impossible, so ecologists use raw data from **quadrats** and **belt transects** to **estimate** population size. The key steps are to calculate the **mean number per quadrat**, scale it up using **population = mean per quadrat x (total area / area of one quadrat)**, and take care with units such as m2 and hectares. You must also be able to work with percentage cover and frequency, spot anomalies, read transect data, and explain why an estimate is only as good as the sampling behind it.

core.p: A **population** is all the organisms of one species living in an area. In a field there may be tens of thousands of daisies, so counting them all would take far too long and would trample the habitat. Instead we count organisms in a small number of **samples** and **scale up** to the whole area.
bullets: Sampling is quicker and causes less damage than counting everything
The estimate assumes the samples are **representative** of the whole area
This is why quadrats must be placed **randomly** (to avoid bias) and in **large numbers**
The answer is always an **estimate**, never an exact count
The same method is used to compare populations in different areas or at different times

callouts.p: Estimated population = mean number per quadrat x (total area / area of one quadrat)

core.h: Types of raw data from field work
core.p: The data you collect depends on the organism. Each type of raw data is processed in a different way, so read the question carefully to see which you have been given.
bullets: **Counts**: the number of individuals in each quadrat (good for plants that are easy to separate, such as daisies or dandelions)
**Percentage cover**: the percentage of the quadrat area covered by a species (used for grass, moss or clover, where individuals are hard to count)
**Presence or absence**: whether the species is in the quadrat or not, used to work out **frequency**
Transect data: counts or cover at each **distance** along a line, alongside an **abiotic** reading

head: Type of data
What you record
What you calculate
rows: Mean per quadrat, density, total population
Count or cover at each distance
Mean at each distance, graph of trend

core.p: The first step is almost always to find the **mean** number of organisms per quadrat. Add up all the counts and divide by the **number of quadrats**, including any quadrats with zero organisms.
bullets: Mean = total number counted / number of quadrats
**Include zeros**: a quadrat with no organisms is still a valid result
Leave out a clear **anomaly** only if there is a good reason, and say so
Keep extra decimal places until the final answer to avoid rounding errors
Give the final answer to a sensible number of **significant figures**

callouts.p: If 10 quadrats were used and two had no plants, you still divide by 10, not 8. Dividing by 8 overestimates the population.

core.p: As well as the mean, exam questions may ask for other ways to summarise quadrat data. Each tells you something slightly different.
bullets: **Mean**: total / number of quadrats; used for scaling up to a population
**Median**: the middle value when the counts are put in order; less affected by one very high or low quadrat
**Mode**: the most common count
**Range**: highest minus lowest value; shows how **spread out** the data is
A large range means organisms are **unevenly distributed** (clumped), so more quadrats are needed for a reliable mean

callouts.p: For the median, always rewrite the numbers in order first. With an even number of values, take the mean of the middle two.

core.p: **Population density** is the number of organisms per unit area, usually per m2. It lets you compare areas sampled with different-sized quadrats.
bullets: Density = mean number per quadrat / area of one quadrat (m2)
A 0.5 m x 0.5 m quadrat has an area of **0.25 m2**, so it fits **4 times** into 1 m2
Example: mean of 6 per 0.25 m2 quadrat = 6 / 0.25 = **24 per m2**
A 1 m x 1 m quadrat has an area of 1 m2, so the mean is already the density
Then: population = density x total area

callouts.t: 0.5 m x 0.5 m is not 0.5 m2
callouts.p: 0.5 x 0.5 = 0.25 m2. Using 0.5 m2 by mistake halves your population estimate.

core.p: To estimate the population of the whole area, scale up the mean using the ratio of the total area to the area of one quadrat. This ratio tells you **how many quadrats would fit** into the whole area.
bullets: Step 1: find the **total area** of the habitat (e.g. length x width)
Step 2: find the **area of one quadrat** in the same units
Step 3: total area / quadrat area = number of quadrats that would fit
Step 4: population = mean per quadrat x number of quadrats that fit
Example: field 50 m x 20 m = 1000 m2; quadrat 0.25 m2; 1000 / 0.25 = 4000; mean 6; population = 6 x 4000 = **24 000**
Check: density 24 per m2 x 1000 m2 = 24 000, the same answer

callouts.p: Estimated population size = mean number of organisms per quadrat x (total area / area of one quadrat)
